subject: Islamic Studies
board: TGA Islamic Studies scheme (aqeedah, fiqh, seerah, hadith, akhlaq)
source: Drive: RE folder and Islamic Studies schemes folder checked (Edexcel Int. GCSE Islamic Studies spec and KS4 SOW only; no KS3 Islamic material) - adapted to the TGA Islamic Studies scheme as a bridge to the Edexcel spec (1.9, 2.1, 2.4, 2.5, 3.3), own knowledge, authentic sources only

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Aqeedah - knowing Allah, the Last Day and al-Qadr
lessons.title: Allah’s names and attributes: the methodology of ahl as-sunnah
objectives: Explain the four principles for approaching Allah’s attributes
Apply the methodology to examples from the Qur’an
Contrast it with the errors of likening and denial

keywords.def: distorting the meaning of a revealed text
asking or claiming to know ‘how’ an attribute is

starter: Define Tawhid and name its three categories.

teach.heading: The starting point
bullets: Allah knows Himself best: “Do you know better than Allah?” (2:140)
We take our knowledge of Him only from the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah
We follow the way of the Companions
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Make clear that ahl as-sunnah wa’l-jama’ah are those who hold to the Qur’an and Sunnah as understood by the Companions and the first generations. Ask: why is the best source of knowledge about Allah the words of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ?

teach.heading: Four principles
bullets: No tahrif: do not distort the meaning
No ta’til: do not deny the attributes
No takyif: do not ask or claim ‘how’
No tamthil: do not liken Allah to creation
teach.note: Write the four on the board. Give the parallel: ‘We believe as Allah described Himself, in a way that suits His majesty.’ Misconception: ‘If we affirm the attribute, we are comparing.’ Respond: affirming that Allah hears does not make His hearing like ours (42:11).

teach.heading: Examples
bullets: Allah speaks: He spoke to Musa directly (4:164)
Allah hears and sees (20:46)
Ar-Rahman rose above the Throne in a way that befits Him (20:5)
Allah’s hand and face are affirmed as He described
teach.note: Use these cautiously and only as verse examples. Teach that we affirm the meaning that Arabic conveys, and leave the ‘how’ to Allah. If asked tricky questions, tell pupils that excessive speculation is discouraged and they can ask their teacher. Do not quote scholars unless sure; stress the principles are drawn from the verses.

teach.heading: Names that fit Allah’s majesty
bullets: Al-Quddus, As-Salam: perfect and free of flaw
Al-Hayy, Al-Qayyum: ever-living, self-sustaining
Al-Aliyy, Al-Azim: the Most High, the Most Great
teach.note: Ayat al-Kursi (2:255) can be read together. Ask pupils to connect each name with how it makes them feel and act: reverence, hope, reliance. The aim is love and fear of Allah in balance, not argument.

practice: Name the four principles and define each in your own words.
Apply the four principles to the statement ‘Allah hears’.
Identify which error is made: ‘Allah’s hand means only power, not a hand’.
independent: Create a table of the four errors with an example and a correct statement for each.
Write a 120-word explanation of 42:11 for a Year 7 pupil.
Write a reflection: how does knowing Allah improve worship?
exit: What does takyif mean?
Why do Muslims avoid comparing Allah to creation?
lessons.homework: Write a one-page summary of the ahl as-sunnah approach to Allah’s attributes with two verses.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded term cards; stretch: respond in writing to the question ‘Why do we not ask how?’

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Aqeedah - knowing Allah, the Last Day and al-Qadr
lessons.title: The Akhirah: death, the grave and the Last Day
objectives: Describe the stages from death to Paradise or Hell
Explain the purpose of accountability
Explain how belief in the Akhirah shapes behaviour

keywords.def: the barrier: the stage between death and resurrection
the scale on which deeds are weighed

starter: List the six pillars of iman.
Why does accountability matter in a fair society?

teach.heading: Death and the grave
bullets: “Every soul will taste death” (3:185)
In the grave, the believer is questioned about Lord, religion and prophet
Allah keeps believers firm (14:27)
The grave is the first stage of the Akhirah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Keep calm and hopeful. 14:27 is explained in Bukhari as referring to the questioning in the grave. The questioning by two angels is in authentic hadith (Abu Dawud and others). Ask: what are the three questions? Why would a believer be able to answer? (The life they lived.)

teach.heading: Signs and the Hour
bullets: Minor signs came first, some already seen
Major signs include the Dajjal, the return of Isa and the sun rising from the west
Only Allah knows when the Hour will come (7:187)
teach.note: The sun rising from the west is in Bukhari and Muslim (Abu Hurayrah). Do not dwell on speculation; the Prophet ﷺ told us to prepare, not to predict. Ask: why do you think Allah hid the time?

teach.heading: Resurrection and judgment
bullets: All creation will be raised
Deeds are weighed with perfect justice (21:47)
People receive their record in the right or left hand (69:19-26)
No one is wronged even by an atom’s weight
teach.note: Edexcel 2.5 passage 101:1-11: those with heavy scales have a pleasant life. Ask: what does ‘heavy scales’ mean? (Good deeds outweigh bad by Allah’s mercy and justice.) Mention that the Prophet ﷺ will intercede by Allah’s permission (Bukhari, Muslim).

teach.heading: Jannah and Jahannam
bullets: Jannah: eternal reward with the pleasure of Allah
The greatest reward is seeing Allah (75:22-23)
Jahannam: punishment for those who reject and wrong
Allah’s mercy is wide (7:156)
teach.note: Handle with maturity; avoid graphic detail. The hadith that ‘My mercy overcomes My anger’ is in Bukhari and Muslim (Abu Hurayrah). Emphasise that we ask Allah for Paradise and refuge from the Fire.

teach.heading: Living with the Akhirah in mind
bullets: Be honest, since deeds are recorded
Make tawbah quickly
Do not be attached to the dunya
Do good in secret
teach.note: Ask pupils to turn belief into action. Example: a pupil sees someone’s dropped wallet. How does belief in the Akhirah guide the choice? Link to the hadith of intentions.

practice: Put the stages in order: death, grave, resurrection, weighing of deeds, Jannah or Jahannam.
Explain what the Mizan shows about Allah.
Give two effects belief in the Akhirah has on behaviour.
independent: Make a flow chart of the journey from death to the final destination with Qur’an references.
Write a 150-word explanation of 101:1-11.
Write a paragraph: ‘Is belief in life after death important for a just society?’
exit: What is Barzakh?
Give one reason why belief in the Last Day matters.
lessons.homework: Write six sentences on how the Akhirah shapes choices in a typical week.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards for the stages; stretch: evaluate arguments for and against belief in resurrection from a Muslim viewpoint.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Aqeedah - knowing Allah, the Last Day and al-Qadr
lessons.title: Al-Qadr: divine decree and human responsibility
objectives: Explain the four levels of belief in al-Qadr
Explain how free will and responsibility relate to Allah’s decree
Respond to the claim that al-Qadr means people have no choice

keywords.def: Allah’s decree and perfect knowledge of everything
creation: Allah created all things and actions

starter: List the stages of the Akhirah.
What does the hadith of intentions teach?

teach.heading: What is al-Qadr?
bullets: “Indeed, We created everything with decree” (54:49)
The sixth pillar of iman
Belief that Allah’s knowledge and will encompass everything
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. In the hadith of Jibril the Prophet ﷺ included belief in al-Qadr, its good and bad (Muslim). Ask: what is the difference between knowing something and forcing it? Use a teacher who knows who will revise.

teach.heading: The four levels
bullets: Knowledge: Allah knows everything before it happens
Writing: Allah wrote it in the Preserved Tablet
Will: nothing occurs unless Allah wills
Creation: Allah created all things, including our abilities
teach.note: Muslim records that Allah wrote the decrees of creation fifty thousand years before creating the heavens and earth. Qur’an 81:29: ‘You do not will except that Allah wills.’ Ask pupils to give an example for each level.

teach.heading: Free will and responsibility
bullets: “Whoever wills, let him believe; whoever wills, let him disbelieve” (18:29)
We choose; Allah knew what we would choose
We are accountable for our choices
We do not know what is written, so we strive
teach.note: This is the essence of the Edexcel 2.4 passage: Ali narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said everyone’s place is written, and when the Companions asked whether they should rely on it, he said ‘Work, for everyone is made easy for what he was created for’ (Bukhari, Muslim). Use this to rebut fatalism. Ask: why does a student still revise even though the result is already known to Allah?

teach.heading: Practical effects
bullets: Effort: take the means
Contentment after effort
Gratitude when good, patience when hard
Do not say ‘if only’ about what is past
teach.note: Hadith in Muslim (Abu Hurayrah): the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer; be keen on what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and if something befalls you do not say ‘if only I had...’, but say ‘Qadar Allah wa ma sha’a fa’al’ (Allah decreed and what He willed He did). Ask pupils to use it in a real example.

teach.heading: Misunderstandings
bullets: Al-Qadr is not an excuse for sin
Knowing is not forcing
Allah is just and does not wrong anyone (4:40)
We ask Allah for guidance daily (1:6)
teach.note: Present the objection: ‘If Allah knows I will fail, why try?’ Reply with the hadith above and the idea of ‘ease towards what we strive for’. Another objection: ‘Why does Allah allow bad people?’ Preview next lesson.

practice: Name the four levels of al-Qadr.
Explain how both Allah’s knowledge and human choice are true.
Respond to this: ‘I will fail whatever I do, as Allah has written it.’
independent: Create an annotated diagram of the four levels with an example for each.
Write a 200-word answer: ‘How can Muslims believe in al-Qadr and free will?’
Write dialogue between two friends discussing the objection.
exit: What is al-Qadr?
Why does belief in al-Qadr not remove responsibility?
lessons.homework: Learn 18:29 and 54:49 and write a short paragraph linking them.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: step diagram with sentence stems; stretch: write a structured 12-mark style evaluation using different viewpoints.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Aqeedah - knowing Allah, the Last Day and al-Qadr
lessons.title: Why is there evil and suffering?
objectives: Explain Muslim responses to evil and suffering
Use Qur’an and hadith to support answers
Evaluate different explanations
starter: What is the difference between sabr and giving up?

teach.heading: The question
bullets: If Allah is Merciful and Almighty, why do people suffer?
Edexcel asks about the nature of evil and suffering
Muslims respond with the Qur’an and Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Be sensitive: some pupils may have lived loss. Acknowledge that suffering is real and that grief is allowed (the Prophet ﷺ wept at the death of his son Ibrahim; Bukhari and Muslim). Ask the class for ways people respond to suffering.

teach.heading: Life is a test
bullets: “We will surely test you with fear, hunger, loss” (2:155)
“Give good news to the patient” (2:155)
Testing shows who is sincere
The test is also for the people around the sufferer
teach.note: Link to 67:2: Allah created death and life to test which of you is best in deeds. Ask: how can suffering reveal compassion in others? Mention that the Prophets faced the hardest tests (Bukhari).

teach.heading: Hardship has wisdom
bullets: It can wipe away sins
It can raise a person in rank
It can bring people back to Allah
“With hardship comes ease” (94:5-6)
teach.note: Abu Sa’id (Bukhari, Muslim): no hardship, illness, worry, grief or even a thorn pricks a believer but Allah expiates some of his sins by it. Ask: how can this help someone who is ill? Make clear that we still seek treatment and help, and do not seek hardship.

teach.heading: Human choices and evil
bullets: Many harms come from human injustice
Free will allows both good and evil
Allah is not unjust to anyone (4:40)
Justice will be completed in the Akhirah
teach.note: Distinguish natural suffering (earthquakes) from moral evil. The Qur’an 30:41 says corruption appears on land and sea because of what people’s hands have earned. We must stop injustice. Evil exists as a test and is part of a wise design; evil is not the aim of Allah’s actions. The Prophet ﷺ taught in du’a, ‘and evil is not attributed to You’ (Muslim).

teach.heading: Responding well
bullets: “Amazing is the believer’s affair” (Muslim, Suhayb)
Be patient in hardship and grateful in ease
Say “Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji’un” (2:156)
Support those who suffer
teach.note: Edexcel 12-mark questions require developed reasons and different views. Give pupils a model paragraph: point, evidence, explanation, a different view (a non-religious view that suffering shows there is no God), and a Muslim response. Compare.

practice: Give two reasons why Muslims believe Allah allows suffering.
Explain the hadith about expiation of sins.
Write one sentence a Muslim might say to someone who is grieving.
independent: Plan and write a 12-mark style answer: ‘Evil and suffering show that Allah does not exist.’ Include a Muslim view and a different view.
Create a poster: ‘How Muslims respond to hardship’.
Write a letter of comfort to a person facing a hard time using the Qur’an and Sunnah.
exit: Name two Muslim responses to suffering.
Which verse says ‘with hardship comes ease’?
lessons.homework: Complete the 12-mark style answer if unfinished, with at least two pieces of evidence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: model paragraph with highlighted structure; stretch: compare Muslim and non-religious responses to suffering with balanced evaluation.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Seerah - the Prophet as leader
lessons.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
objectives: Explain why the Prophet ﷺ set out for Umrah
Describe the terms of the treaty
Assess why it was called a clear victory

keywords.def: a place near Makkah where the treaty was signed in 6 AH
the pledge of allegiance under the tree

starter: Who won the Battle of Badr?
How many years after the Hijrah was Hudaybiyyah?

teach.heading: The journey for Umrah
bullets: In 6 AH the Prophet ﷺ set out with about 1,400 Companions
They wore ihram and carried no war weapons
Quraysh blocked them from Makkah
They camped at Hudaybiyyah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Bukhari reports about 1,400 in the pledge. Explain they intended peace. Ask: what shows peaceful intent? (Sacrificial animals, ihram.) The Prophet ﷺ had a dream of entering Makkah, and the Muslims were eager.

teach.heading: Negotiations and the pledge
bullets: Uthman was sent to negotiate
A rumour spread that he was killed
The Companions pledged under the tree (48:18)
Allah was pleased with the believers
teach.note: 48:18: ‘Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.’ Ask: what does this show about their loyalty? The rumour proved false and Uthman returned.

teach.heading: The terms
bullets: A ten-year truce
The Muslims return this year, perform Umrah the next year
Quraysh men who joined Muslims without a guardian’s permission were returned
Tribes could ally with either side
teach.note: Bukhari and Muslim narrate the terms and the Companions’ dislike of the apparent unfairness. Umar asked difficult questions; reports say he later regretted his strong words and did many good deeds in response. The Prophet ﷺ trusted Allah’s plan. Ask: why did the Companions find it hard?

teach.heading: A clear victory
bullets: Surah al-Fath (48) was revealed on the way back
“Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest” (48:1)
Peace allowed people to meet Muslims and hear the message
Many people accepted Islam in the next two years
teach.note: Bukhari records the revelation of 48:1 on the return, and Umar’s surprise. Ask pupils to explain how a treaty that seemed to disadvantage Muslims could be a victory. Mention that after it, great figures like Khalid ibn al-Walid and Amr ibn al-As accepted Islam. Also letters were sent to rulers.

teach.heading: Lessons in leadership
bullets: Patience and long-term vision
Honour agreements
Seek peace where possible (8:61)
Consult but trust revelation
teach.note: Edexcel 1.7 relevance: relationships with other communities. Ask: what makes a strong leader at school or in a business? Compare with the Prophet ﷺ.

practice: List three terms of the treaty.
Why were the Companions unhappy?
Why did Allah call it a clear conquest?
independent: Write a balanced paragraph: ‘Did Hudaybiyyah benefit the Muslims?’
Create a timeline from the departure to the treaty.
Write a speech by Umar reflecting on the treaty.
exit: Which surah was revealed on the way back from Hudaybiyyah?
Give one benefit of the treaty.
lessons.homework: Use the PEEL structure to answer: ‘How did the treaty of Hudaybiyyah help the spread of Islam?’
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: cause and effect chain; stretch: evaluate whether the treaty was more a diplomatic or religious success.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Seerah - the Prophet as leader
lessons.title: The Conquest of Makkah and forgiveness
objectives: Explain why the Muslims marched on Makkah
Describe the entry into Makkah
Evaluate the Prophet’s ﷺ treatment of his enemies

keywords.def: the conquest of Makkah in Ramadan 8 AH
a tribe allied to the Muslims
the surah about Allah’s help and victory

starter: Name one term of the Hudaybiyyah treaty.
Which Companion negotiated at Hudaybiyyah on the Muslims’ behalf?

teach.heading: The treaty is broken
bullets: An ally of Quraysh attacked Khuza’ah, an ally of the Muslims
Quraysh helped with weapons
The treaty was broken
Quraysh sent Abu Sufyan to renew it but failed
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: why did the Prophet ﷺ respond? (He had to protect an ally under the treaty.) Link to honouring agreements from the previous lesson.

teach.heading: The march
bullets: About 10,000 Muslims marched in Ramadan 8 AH
The army moved in secret
They camped near Makkah and lit many fires
Abu Sufyan embraced Islam
teach.note: From the seerah. The Prophet ﷺ gave an assurance: whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan, or closes his door, or enters the Masjid al-Haram is safe (Muslim). Ask: how does this reduce bloodshed?

teach.heading: Entering Makkah
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ entered with his head bowed in humility
There was little fighting
He cleansed the Ka’bah of idols
“Truth has come and falsehood has vanished” (17:81)
teach.note: Bukhari reports he recited 17:81 as he struck the idols with a stick. Ask: how would you feel returning to a city that drove you out? Contrast the humility with the usual victor’s arrogance.

teach.heading: Forgiveness
bullets: The Quraysh feared revenge
The Prophet ﷺ forgave them
Most accepted Islam
Bilal gave the adhan from the Ka’bah
teach.note: Say ‘reports in the seerah state’ about his address to the Quraysh and his pardon. Mention that a few individuals were named as exceptions due to serious crimes, though several were forgiven. Do not quote exact words of the address. Ask: what does forgiveness do to enemies?

teach.heading: Surah an-Nasr and its lessons
bullets: “When the victory of Allah and the conquest comes” (110:1)
People entered Islam in crowds
The response: glorify Allah and seek forgiveness
Victory should bring humility
teach.note: Link to Edexcel 1.7: treatment of opponents. Ask pupils to write a short assessment of the Prophet ﷺ as a military and moral leader. Compare with conquests that ended in revenge.

practice: Why did the Muslims march on Makkah?
Describe how the Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah.
What does Surah an-Nasr teach about victory?
independent: Write a 12-mark style response: ‘The conquest of Makkah shows the Prophet ﷺ was a great leader.’ Argue both sides.
Create a storyboard of the entry with captions.
Write a diary entry of someone from Quraysh on that day.
exit: In which month did the conquest happen?
Name one way the Prophet ﷺ showed mercy.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph comparing the Prophet’s ﷺ entry into Makkah with a modern leader’s victory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sentence starters for evaluation; stretch: analyse why forgiveness was politically and spiritually wise.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Seerah - the Prophet as leader
lessons.title: The Farewell Pilgrimage and Sermon
objectives: Describe the Prophet’s ﷺ last Hajj
State the main themes of the Farewell Sermon
Explain the significance of 5:3

keywords.def: the plain where the pilgrims gather on the 9th of Dhu’l-Hijjah

starter: Name two lessons from the conquest of Makkah.

teach.heading: The last Hajj
bullets: In 10 AH the Prophet ﷺ performed Hajj
Thousands of Muslims joined him
He taught the rituals: “Take your rites from me”
The details of Hajj were taught through his example
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Jabir’s long hadith in Sahih Muslim describes the Hajj. ‘Take your rites from me’ is also in Muslim. Ask: why is it important that the Prophet ﷺ taught directly? Link to Sunnah as explanation.

teach.heading: The sermon at Arafat
bullets: Your lives and wealth are sacred
The riba of the days of ignorance is abolished
Treat women with kindness and fear Allah regarding them
Hold fast to the Book of Allah
teach.note: From Muslim (Jabir). He said that the blood and wealth are sacred as this day, this month, this city. He abolished pre-Islamic blood feuds and riba. He asked: have I conveyed? and the people replied yes, and he said ‘O Allah, bear witness’.

teach.heading: Equality and justice
bullets: “No Arab is superior to a non-Arab” except by taqwa (Ahmad)
All people descend from Adam
No racism or tribal pride
Everyone is accountable to Allah
teach.note: This wording is in Musnad Ahmad and is graded authentic. Link to 49:13. Ask: how does the sermon challenge racism today? Edexcel 1.6: human rights and equality.

teach.heading: The religion is complete
bullets: “Today I have perfected your religion for you” (5:3)
Revealed on the day of Arafat
The message was complete and delivered
Revealed while the Prophet ﷺ was at Arafat
teach.note: Edexcel passage 5:3. Bukhari reports that a Jewish man told Umar of this verse and Umar said we know the day and place where it was revealed: Arafat on a Friday. Ask: what does ‘perfected’ mean? (No new revelation or religion will be added.)

teach.heading: After the sermon
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ returned to Madinah
Soon after, he became ill
He passed away in the home of Aisha in 11 AH
Muslims were devastated; Abu Bakr steadied them with the Qur’an
teach.note: Abu Bakr’s words in Bukhari: ‘Whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is ever-living and never dies,’ then he recited 3:144. Treat with respect. Ask: how did this strengthen the community's faith?

practice: List four themes of the Farewell Sermon.
Explain what 5:3 teaches about the religion.
Why did Abu Bakr quote 3:144?
independent: Write a 150-word summary of the sermon highlighting human rights.
Prepare a 6-mark style answer: ‘Explain why the Farewell Sermon is important for Muslims.’
Create a poster showing equality in the sermon.
exit: Where was the sermon delivered?
Name one right mentioned in the sermon.
lessons.homework: Compare one theme of the sermon with a modern human-rights principle and explain similarities.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: simplified sermon extracts and glossary; stretch: evaluate how the sermon summarises the Prophet’s ﷺ achievements.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Hadith, fiqh and the law
lessons.title: How hadith were collected and graded
objectives: Explain how hadith were preserved and recorded
State the conditions for an authentic hadith
Name the major collections and their compilers

keywords.def: authentic: connected chain of upright, accurate narrators, without hidden defect
narrated by so many that agreement on lying is impossible

starter: Why do we not share unchecked quotes?

teach.heading: Preserving the Sunnah
bullets: Companions memorised and acted on the Sunnah
Some, like Abdullah ibn Amr, wrote hadith down
Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz encouraged official compilation
Scholars travelled for a single narration
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Abdullah ibn Amr’s written book is mentioned in Bukhari (Abu Hurayrah). Ask: why would scholars travel for one hadith? (To check its chain.) Edexcel 1.5b: recording the Sunnah.

teach.heading: Conditions of a sahih hadith
bullets: A connected chain
Narrators upright in character
Narrators with accurate memory
No hidden defect and no conflict with stronger reports
teach.note: Write the five conditions: ittisal, ‘adalah, dabt, no shudhudh, no illah. Keep the Arabic terms for stretch pupils. Use a courtroom analogy: witnesses must be honest and accurate.

teach.heading: Collections and compilers
bullets: Bukhari (d. 256 AH) and Muslim (d. 261 AH)
Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa’i, Ibn Majah
Malik’s Muwatta’ and Ahmad’s Musnad
Bukhari and Muslim did not include every authentic hadith
teach.note: Imam Bukhari reportedly selected from hundreds of thousands of narrations; say ‘reportedly’. Ask: how do you think a collection is organised? (By chapters/topics.) Show how to cite a hadith, for example ‘Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1’.

teach.heading: Dealing with weak and fabricated reports
bullets: “Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire”
Fabricated reports are not Sunnah
Be careful with quotes in social media
Ask: where is it from? Is it graded?
teach.note: The hadith is mutawatir (Bukhari, Muslim). Provide a method: 1) find the source; 2) find the grading by a reliable scholar; 3) if unsure, do not share. Never invent reports.

teach.heading: Using hadith in an exam
bullets: Quote briefly and accurately
Name the narrator or collection if you know it
Explain meaning and relevance
Link to a belief or practice
teach.note: Edexcel questions use given passages; practise a short paragraph: quote, explain, apply. Model on the board.

practice: List the conditions of a sahih hadith.
Name two scholars who compiled authentic hadith.
Explain why the isnad system is important.
independent: Create a flow chart: how to check a hadith before sharing.
Write a 6-mark style answer: ‘Explain how the Sunnah was recorded.’
Prepare a mini-biography of Imam al-Bukhari or Imam Muslim from reliable sources.
exit: Name two conditions of a sahih hadith.
What should you do before sharing a hadith online?
lessons.homework: Find one hadith quoted in a book or website and trace its collection and grading.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: vocabulary matching; stretch: discuss how modern technology helps or harms hadith verification.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Hadith, fiqh and the law
lessons.title: The four schools of fiqh and the etiquette of differing
objectives: Name the four Sunni schools and their founders
Explain why scholars differ
Show respect for valid differences

keywords.def: following a qualified scholar’s ruling without knowing the evidence

starter: Name the four sources of Shari’ah.

teach.heading: The four imams
bullets: Abu Hanifa (d. 150 AH)
Malik ibn Anas (d. 179 AH)
Ash-Shafi’i (d. 204 AH)
Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH)
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The four schools: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali. Malik wrote the Muwatta’ in Madinah; Ahmad compiled the Musnad. Each used the Qur’an, Sunnah and consensus, with differing methods. Ask: where do your families’ practices come from?

teach.heading: Why do scholars differ?
bullets: Different readings of the Arabic wording
A hadith reached one scholar, but not another
Different grading of a hadith
Different ways to combine texts
teach.note: Give a simple example: whether touching a spouse breaks wudu. Different scholars understood the evidence differently. These are secondary matters; core beliefs (Tawhid, salah, fasting) are agreed upon.

teach.heading: A lesson from the Prophet ﷺ
bullets: At Banu Qurayzah, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Let none pray Asr except at Banu Qurayzah”
Some prayed on the way; others delayed
He did not blame either group (Bukhari, Muslim)
teach.note: Use this to teach adab of ikhtilaf. Both groups acted from sincere understanding. Ask: how should this shape the way we speak about people who follow another valid opinion?

teach.heading: Adab of disagreement
bullets: Respect scholars of other schools
Do not mock or insult
Distinguish core beliefs from open questions
Ask qualified scholars
teach.note: Differences in aqeedah foundations are not the same as differences in minor fiqh; ahl as-sunnah hold firm on fundamentals while tolerating valid differences in branches. Make this clear to pupils but keep it simple.

teach.heading: Applying this
bullets: At home, follow your family’s school as a learner
Do not argue about small differences at the masjid
Focus on shared duties: salah, honesty, kindness
teach.note: Role play: two pupils pray with different hand positions; how do they speak? Show a gentle response.

practice: Match each school with its founder.
Give two reasons scholars differ.
What lesson do we learn from the Banu Qurayzah hadith?
independent: Create a fact file on one imam from reliable sources.
Write a 6-mark style response: ‘Explain why Muslims may follow different schools of law.’
Write dialogue showing good manners when disagreeing.
exit: Name the four schools.
Give one rule for respectful disagreement.
lessons.homework: Ask a family member which school they follow and what they know about its founder.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline of the four imams; stretch: discuss when disagreement is acceptable and when it is not.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Hadith, fiqh and the law
lessons.title: Sawm: the rules and spirit of fasting
objectives: State the rules of fasting in Ramadan
Explain who is exempt and what they must do
Explain the spiritual aims of fasting

keywords.def: the meal to break the fast
feeding a poor person for each missed day when unable to make up

starter: What happened in Ramadan to make it special?

teach.heading: The command to fast
bullets: “Fasting is prescribed for you ... that you may become mindful of Allah” (2:183)
Ramadan is when the Qur’an was revealed (2:185)
Fasting is a shield and a form of taqwa
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 3.3 passage 2:183-185. Highlight that the aim is taqwa. The Prophet ﷺ said fasting is a shield (Bukhari, Muslim). Ask: what is the shield from?

teach.heading: What is required
bullets: Intention before Fajr
Abstain from food, drink and intimacy from dawn to sunset
Avoid lying, arguing and bad speech
“Whoever does not give up false speech ... Allah has no need for his leaving food and drink” (Bukhari)
teach.note: Explain the intention (niyyah) in the heart. The hadith is narrated by Abu Hurayrah. Clarify: eating or drinking by mistake does not break the fast (Bukhari, Muslim). Ask: how can social media be part of ‘false speech’?

teach.heading: Exemptions and make-up
bullets: The sick and travellers: make up the days later (2:184)
The elderly or permanently ill: feed a poor person for each day
Women with menstruation or post-natal bleeding must make up the days
Children are not obliged but encouraged
teach.note: Scholars differ on details for pregnant and nursing women (make up, or feed, or both); tell pupils to consult a scholar. Emphasise ease: ‘Allah intends ease for you’ (2:185). Ask: how does Islam show mercy here?

teach.heading: Sunnah etiquette
bullets: Suhoor has blessing (Bukhari, Muslim)
Hasten to break the fast (Bukhari, Muslim)
Increase Qur’an, du’a and charity
Seek Laylat al-Qadr in the last ten nights
teach.note: Anas: ‘Take suhoor, for in suhoor there is blessing.’ Sahl ibn Sa’d: people remain in good as long as they hasten the iftar. Laylat al-Qadr: better than a thousand months (97:3) - Edexcel 1.2 link. Ask pupils to plan a Ramadan routine.

teach.heading: Spiritual aims
bullets: Self-control
Empathy for the hungry
Gratitude
Community and generosity
teach.note: Give the challenge: pick three goals for Ramadan: one for Qur’an, one for character, one for community. Discuss modern issues such as exam-time fasting.

practice: List what breaks the fast and what does not.
Who is exempt and what should they do?
Explain two spiritual benefits of fasting.
independent: Write a Ramadan plan with goals for Qur’an, salah and charity.
Write a 6-mark style answer: ‘Explain the importance of fasting for Muslims.’
Design an information leaflet on fasting for a new Muslim.
exit: What is the aim of fasting in 2:183?
Give one exemption from fasting and what to do instead.
lessons.homework: Write a reflection on how fasting could improve your akhlaq.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: scenario cards (break/not break); stretch: compare fasting with other forms of self-discipline.

lessons.title: Halal earning, honest trade and riba
objectives: Explain Islamic teaching on halal income
Define riba and give examples
Apply honesty in trade to scenarios

keywords.def: usury or interest: an unjust increase on a loan
excessive uncertainty or deception in a contract

teach.heading: Earning honestly
bullets: “No one has eaten better food than that earned by his own hands” (Bukhari)
Narrated by al-Miqdam
Work is honourable, begging is discouraged
The Prophet ﷺ was a trader and shepherd
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Link to al-Amin from Year 6. Ask: how does honest work build dignity? Mention that Dawud (peace be upon him) ate from the work of his hands (Bukhari).

teach.heading: Trade is permitted; riba is forbidden
bullets: “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba” (2:275)
Riba: extra money demanded for a loan
Example: borrow £1,000, repay £1,100 because of delay
It exploits those in need
teach.note: Worked example: Ali borrows £1,000 and must repay £1,100 after a year. The extra £100 is riba. Compare with a sale: a shop buys a bike for £200 and sells for £250, which is permitted trade because of real goods and shared risk. Ask: why is it unjust? (Rich gain, poor suffer.)

teach.heading: Honesty in trade
bullets: “Whoever cheats us is not one of us” (Muslim)
Show defects in goods
Give full measure (83:1-3)
Do not hoard to raise prices
teach.note: The hadith of the wet grain at the bottom of the heap is in Muslim (Abu Hurayrah). Ask pupils to give modern examples: false advertising, fake reviews, selling unsafe goods. Link to amanah.

teach.heading: Other forbidden dealings
bullets: Gambling and games of chance (5:90)
Bribery
Theft and fraud
Selling what is haram
teach.note: Keep concise. Explain the reasoning: these harm individuals and society. Encourage fair business ethics such as fair wages and paying on time. Use the Qur’anic principle of justice (4:29: do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly).

teach.heading: A good earner
bullets: Seek halal earnings
Be generous and pay zakah
Avoid waste (17:26-27)
Trust Allah for provision
teach.note: Ask pupils to design a ‘code of ethics’ for a small online shop. Revisit zakah.

practice: Define riba in your own words.
Identify which scenarios are riba: (a) borrow £500 repay £500 (b) borrow £500 repay £600.
Give two examples of cheating in trade.
independent: Write a code of ethics for a Muslim-owned shop with five rules and a Qur’an or hadith reason for each.
Write a 6-mark style answer: ‘Explain why Islam forbids riba.’
Create a short case study of an honest businessperson from the Companions (from reliable sources).
exit: What does 2:275 say about trade and riba?
Give an example of honest trade.
lessons.homework: Write a short advice letter to a friend starting an online business, using at least two Islamic principles.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: scenario cards with money examples; stretch: evaluate the difference between a loan with interest and a profit-sharing partnership.

lessons.title: Guarding the tongue: backbiting and good speech
objectives: Define backbiting using the hadith
Explain the Qur’anic warning in 49:11-13
Suggest practical ways to guard the tongue

keywords.def: backbiting: mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike, even if true
slander: saying something false about someone

starter: Define riba and give an example.
Quote a hadith about speaking good or keeping silent.

teach.heading: Qur’anic warning
bullets: “Do not spy or backbite each other” (49:12)
“Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?”
Avoid assumptions, mocking and nicknames (49:11-12)
Allah accepts repentance
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Edexcel 2.8 passage 49:11-13. Explain the strong image: backbiting damages a person who cannot defend himself. Ask: why is the image so powerful?

teach.heading: What is backbiting?
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ asked: do you know what backbiting is?
“Your mentioning your brother in a way he dislikes”
If it is true, it is backbiting; if false, it is slander
Narrated by Abu Hurayrah (Muslim)
teach.note: Use the full hadith: a man asked, ‘What if what I say is true?’ and the Prophet ﷺ replied that if it is true you have backbitten him and if it is not true you have slandered him. Ask for school-age examples, e.g. group chat gossip.

teach.heading: Exceptions
bullets: Seeking help against injustice
Asking for a fatwa
Warning others of real harm in a fair way
Not for fun or revenge
teach.note: Scholars mention limited cases where mentioning a person is permissible, such as complaining to someone who can help or a person seeking advice in marriage. Stress that this is for need, not gossip. Remind pupils to ask a teacher if unsure.

teach.heading: The Muslim’s speech
bullets: “A Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand people are safe” (Bukhari, Muslim)
Speak good or be silent
Reconcile between people
Make excuses for others
teach.note: Link to the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr. Mention that Allah praises those who encourage charity, kindness and reconciliation (4:114). Ask: when did you last defend someone behind their back?

teach.heading: Practical steps
bullets: Stop and change the subject
Leave the gathering
Make tawbah and seek forgiveness from the person if possible
Speak well of people in their absence
teach.note: Role play a gossip scenario with pupils choosing responses. Final consolidation: ask pupils to revisit their Year 8 truthfulness goal and add tongue goals. Quick end-of-unit quiz.

practice: Define ghibah and buhtan.
Decide whether it is backbiting: ‘She always comes late’ said when she is absent.
Suggest two ways to respond when others backbite.
independent: Write a short story where a pupil stops a friend from backbiting.
Create a ‘tongue guard’ checklist with five rules.
Write a 6-mark style answer: ‘Explain Islamic teaching about harmful speech.’
exit: Give the hadith definition of backbiting.
Name one exception where mentioning a person is allowed.
lessons.homework: Keep a three-day speech diary noting times you spoke kindly or avoided gossip.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: scenario cards; stretch: analyse online gossip against Islamic principles.
